fetched_contents.text: Non-destructive dendrochronology with X-ray computed tomography: The influence of different conservation methods for waterlogged archaeological wood Under a Creative Commons license Open access Abstract In this study, the influence of different conservation methods for waterlogged archaeological wood (WAW) on non-destructive dendrochronological dating by micro-computed tomography (µCT) was evaluated. For this purpose, samples of different wood species were conserved using the following methods: alcohol-ether-resin, Kauramin 800®, lactitol/trehalose, saccharose, silicone oil and different polyethylene glycol (PEG) treatments with subsequent freeze-drying. The tree ring measurements of all samples in the digital µCT data were compared with the measurements on an analog linear measuring table in terms of the total number of rings per sample and the mean ring width. The year-to-year ring width measurements in the µCT data agreed very well overall with the corresponding microscopic measurements. It was possible to detect the rings in the samples with µCT in all cases. A dendrochronological cross dating with regional absolutely dated ring width chronologies was successful in two cases. However, the different influence of the conservation agents on the quality of the µCT data was clearly visible. In order to assess this influence, the contrast in the µCT data was determined using grey-scale profiles. A decrease in contrast in the µCT data was detectable for all conservation agents. A particular strong influence is observed for the conservation methods using silicone oil, lactitol/trehalose, PEG and saccharose. Overall, the study performed confirms that µCT is a powerful and accurate method for non-destructive dendrochronology of conserved archaeological objects. * Previous * Next Keywords Dendrochronology Conservation Waterlogged archaeological wood Non-destructive analysis X-ray computed tomography 1. Introduction In the temperate zone, archaeological objects made of wood are preserved mainly under waterlogged and anoxic conditions, where microbial decay is slowed down, and the wood structure is more or less completely filled with water. If waterlogged archaeological wood (WAW) is left to dry in an uncontrolled manner after excavation, it may collapse and shrink. Depending on the degree of degradation this can result in a complete loss of the object's original form and information. A lot of methods and conservation agents have already been tested for the conservation of WAW. In addition, there were several studies which aimed to compare the efficiency of the conservation methods (Christensen et al., 2012, Walsh et al., 2014, Walsh et al., 2017, Broda and Hill, 2021, Stelzner et al., 2022). Since plants adapt to environmental conditions during their lifetime and store this information in their tissues, wooden objects contain important evidence for archaeological research. This information enables the reconstruction of the living conditions of trees. Archaeological wood therefore offers an archive for interdisciplinary research. Ecological, economic, vegetation-historical, climatic and cultural-historical questions can be investigated. Furthermore, dendrochronology is a widely used, reliable and very accurate method for dating archaeological wood finds and thus an indispensable tool for archaeological research (Schweingruber, 2001, Baillie, 2002, Hughes, 2002, Speer, 2010, Billamboz, 2014). In general, the width of the annual rings is measured on the cross-section with an accuracy of 1/100 mm (Westphal and Heußner, 2016). If the outermost annual ring has been preserved under the bark (waney edge), both the felling date and the felling time can be determined (Sass-Klaassen et al., 2008). In conventional dendrochronological dating, the artifact must be sawed or drilled with an increment borer in order to get a cross section and measure all tree rings. This contradicts the requirements of conservation, which pursues the aim of preserving the object unchanged and as a whole. Similarly, the preparation of cross-sectional surfaces with a razor blade for dendrochronological dating is an invasive intervention in an artifact (Sass and Eckstein, 1994, Kuniholm, 2001, Bräker, 2002, Westphal and Heußner, 2016). Among the currently available non-destructive methods, X-ray computed tomography (CT) is a suitable technique that allows the entire volume of a sample to be examined at various spatial resolutions (Withers et al., 2021). The method provides promising information to archaeological sciences in the field of dendroarchaeology, including conservation science (Stelzner et al., 2021, Stelzner et al., 2022). Not only is it non-invasive, but it requires almost no sample preparation and allows both qualitative and quantitative three-dimensional tree ring analyses (Van den Bulcke et al., 2014, Martinez-Garcia et al., 2021, Martinez-Garcia et al., 2022). For these reasons, CT has enabled significant progress towards a non-destructive technique in the field of dendrochronology, both for wooden cultural heritage (Okochi, 2016, Daly and Streeton, 2017, Bossema et al., 2021, Domínguez-Delmás et al., 2021) as well as dendroecology and forest sciences (Maes et al., 2017, Vannoppen et al., 2017). The first attempts at non-destructive dendrochronological dating based on CT images were made as early as the 1980 s (Onoe et al., 1984). However, sufficient resolution for non-destructive analysis and successful dating of wood samples was not achieved until the development of industrial µCT (Okochi et al., 2007). As a result in dendroarchaeology, for example, the oak figures from Fellbach-Schmiden could be dated to 127 ± 10 BCE (Keefer et al., 2006) and the oak figure from Eschenz to 9 ± 10 BCE (Belz et al., 2008). fetched_contents.text: Stabilisation of waterlogged archaeological wood: the analysis of structural and dimensional changes of different conservation methods using magnetic resonance imaging and X-ray micro-computed tomography Abstract Waterlogged archaeological wood can be preserved for many years in the absence of air, as decomposition is substantially slowed down. After excavation, conservation is necessary to prevent damage of objects due to uncontrolled drying. In this study, the following conservation methods were tested to investigate their ability to stabilise the objects: alcohol-ether resin, melamine-formaldehyde (Kauramin 800), lactitol/trehalose, saccharose, polyethylene glycol (PEG 2000 with air-drying and PEG 2000 or 400 and 4000 with subsequent freeze-drying). In order to precisely understand the changes caused by conservation and drying, 40 samples each of pine wood and oak wood were documented using magnetic resonance imaging and X-ray micro-computed tomography before and after conservation. This imaging made it possible to quantitatively record changes in the wood structure, for example due to shrinkage, collapse and cracks, which could not be prevented by conservation. The alcohol-ether-resin method with solvent drying had the best stabilizing effect and no damage of the wood structure was visible. The two PEG treatments followed by freeze drying showed effective volume stabilisation. In both cases, however, the treatment led to cracks in the wood structure, which occurred less frequently when the cryoprotectant PEG 400 was used. In comparison, the other methods with air drying did not show consistently good results in stabilizing the volume or wood structure. Keywords: Conservation, Waterlogged archaeological wood, Collapse, Cracks, Volume, Shrinkage, X-ray micro-computed tomography, Magnetic resonance imaging Subject terms: Engineering, Materials science Introduction Wood can be preserved in temperate climate zones in water bodies or water-saturated soils under anoxic conditions over a very long period of time. The degradation of wood under such conditions takes place very slowly and leads to a change in the structure and composition of the objects: Primarily, the cellulose components of the secondary cell wall are decomposed by microorganisms such as fungi (soft-rot fungi (SR)) and bacteria (tunnelling bacteria (TB) and erosion bacteria (EB))1. Furthermore, lignin can be degraded by oxidation and hydrolysis2. This degradation is a common process that leads to decay of the wood, in which ultimately only the skeletal framework of the middle lamella holds the structure together. The secondary cell wall, which is primarily responsible for the stability of the undamaged wood3, then contains only degraded lignin and bacterial slime4. The process can be very heterogeneous and some cells can be degraded while neighbouring cells remain undamaged5. This decomposition, which begins in the outer regions, leads to physical weakening of the structure and to fragility of the archaeological wood during ground deposition6. Water from the environment fills the pore spaces - the capillaries and microcapillaries - and causes the wood structure to swell. Waterlogged archaeological wood (WAW) continues to decompose, and the interaction of microorganisms, fungal attack and chemical reactions with salt and fresh water can increase this decomposition and lead to extensive damage that compromises the structural integrity of the wood remains7. The more cell wall material is broken down, the more water fills the internal cavities. The maximum water content therefore increases as the wood degrades and is an universally used indicator of the state of preservation8. WAW is very sensitive after excavation and can suffer considerable damage within a few hours without protective measures. Due to the increased oxygen supply after excavation, WAW is also susceptible to degradation by oxygen-tolerant microorganisms1 and other oxygen-related degradation processes. If WAW air-dries, capillary forces occur due to the high surface tension of the evaporating water. This causes the cell walls to shrink and the cells to collapse9,10. Depending on the degree of degradation, only a fraction of the wood volume remains. The dimensional changes during drying happen in two stages11: Above the fibre saturation point, degraded cells collapse due to capillary tension and drying stress12,13. Below the fibre saturation point, the cell walls begin to shrink, whereby the volume loss of WAW is proportional to the water content and the shrinkage in tangential direction is generally greater than in radial and longitudinal direction10. Wood has unique material properties and is also readily available and easy to work with. Due to its frequent use and the information stored in wood anatomy, it plays an irreplaceable role in the study of the way of life of people and their environment in the past. This requires the permanent preservation of these unique sources, which has led to the development of methods to prevent uncontrolled drying out14. The damaging effect of air-drying and the question of how to solve this problem was recognized as early as the 19th century as not an easy task15, and since that time a variety of methods and conservation agents have been tested14. Currently there are two different strategies to preserve WAW: the (re-) burial in a protected, natural, anaerobic and waterlogged environment and conservation treatments. To avoid shrinkage, rupture, splits, cracks and collapse of WAW upon drying is the main challenge for the conservation16. In addition to the preservation of cultural heritage, conservation measures are required to minimise the impact on the material properties for possible future investigations17. Micro-CT is positioned as a non-destructive method for examining waterlogged archaeological wood, but the evidence here suggests it is not the only imaging option and that its suitability depends on the research question and available resources.

Compared with X-ray CT, the distinction in the evidence is mainly one of scale and resolution. The N1 evidence says that X-ray computed tomography is a suitable method for examining the entire volume of a sample at various spatial resolutions and that µCT enables non-destructive dendrochronological dating with resolutions down to 0.12 mm [N1-F1]. The N3 evidence adds that micro-CT scanners can take several hours per slice, while medical CT scanners take about one second per slice, though the excerpt does not directly compare micro-CT with X-ray CT as a pair [N3-R3]. Taken together, the evidence supports the idea that micro-CT is more detailed than standard X-ray CT for wood anatomy but slower and more resource-intensive [N1-F1][N3-R3]. For waterlogged wood, this means µCT is better when high-resolution internal structure matters, while X-ray CT may be preferable for quicker volumetric surveys.

Compared with MRI, the evidence is more limited but still informative. The N3 excerpt says MRI is suitable for examining volumetric internal structure of waterlogged wooden objects, but it is typically not used for the same purpose as µCT [N3-R1]. The N1 evidence also notes that µCT is a suitable technique that allows the entire volume of a sample to be examined at various spatial resolutions, while the MRI comparison is only indirect [N1-F1]. So the comparative context is that MRI is a volumetric internal-structure method, but µCT is the preferred modality for archaeologically relevant wood when both non-destructive and detailed anatomy are important [N3-R1][N1-F1]. The evidence does not provide a direct trade-off table, so the safest conclusion is that µCT is more suitable for wood anatomy and conservation monitoring, while MRI is more specialized for soft or hydrated samples where detailed volumetric structure is the priority [N3-R1][N1-F1].

Compared with macroscopic analysis, the evidence emphasizes that µCT provides information that macroscopic analysis alone cannot. The N1 evidence states that conventional dendrochronological dating requires sawing or drilling to get a cross section and measure tree rings, which contradicts conservation aims [N1-F1]. The same source also says µCT provides promising information to archaeological sciences in dendroarchaeology and conservation science and allows both qualitative and quantitative three-dimensional tree ring analyses [N1-F1]. The N2 evidence similarly frames µCT as part of a comprehensive analysis of structures, porosity, water distribution, decay, and structural inclusions [N2-R1]. So macroscopic analysis is limited by surface access and destructive sampling, whereas µCT is non-invasive and can capture internal features invisible to the naked eye [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The trade-off is that macroscopic methods may be faster and cheaper, but µCT is more informative for internal decay, anatomy, and conservation assessment [N1-F1][N2-R1].

On trade-offs between speed, cost, and detail, the evidence is clear. µCT is slower than medical CT and may take several hours per slice [N3-R3], and the N1 evidence says it is a suitable method that can be used to examine the entire volume of a sample but does not explicitly say it is fast [N1-F1]. Cost is not directly quantified in the provided evidence, so it should be treated as a practical variable rather than a factual comparison. For detail, the evidence repeatedly points to µCT’s ability to visualize internal structure, tree rings, and conservation changes with high resolution [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The main implication is that µCT is more suitable when the research question asks about internal anatomy, decay, conservation effects, or tree-ring details; it is less suitable when a quick, low-resolution survey or only surface-level inspection is sufficient [N1-F1][N3-R3].

On when micro-CT is more or less suitable than other modalities, the evidence supports a conditional choice. It is more suitable than macroscopic analysis when internal structure matters [N1-F1][N2-R1], more suitable than MRI when the goal is high-resolution wood anatomy rather than purely volumetric soft-tissue imaging [N3-R1], and more suitable than standard X-ray CT when higher spatial resolution is needed [N1-F1][N3-R3]. It is less suitable when rapid scanning is required or when the object is too fragile for the scanning process itself. The evidence also suggests it is less suitable than some alternative conservation methods for long-term preservation, but that is a conservation issue rather than an imaging issue [N4-F2][N6-R1]. Overall, µCT is best when non-destructive, high-resolution internal imaging of waterlogged wood is needed, and less appropriate when the question is purely surface-level or when speed is the main constraint [N1-F1][N3-R3][N3-R1].

The practical applications of micro-CT for archaeological wood are broad and centered on the fact that it can examine internal structure without cutting or damaging the object. The evidence shows that micro-CT is used for comprehensive analysis of structures, porosity, water distribution, decay, and structural inclusions in waterlogged wood [N2-R1]. It is also used to analyze dimensional stability after conservation, which is relevant to understanding how the wood changed during drying and treatment [N2-R2]. In dendrochronology, the evidence is especially strong: µCT enables non-destructive dendrochronological dating with resolutions down to 0.12 mm, and the study found that µCT data agreed very well with microscopic measurements for tree ring count and mean ring width [N1-F1]. It also notes that µCT can detect rings in all samples and supports cross dating with regional chronologies [N1-F1].

For species identification and provenance analysis, the evidence is indirect but plausible. Since µCT can capture internal anatomy, vessel structure, and wood morphology, it is well suited to identifying species and inferring provenance because wood anatomy is a key identifier for taxonomy and environmental context [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The N2 evidence explicitly states that microCT imaging is used in archaeobotanical research, which implies that it can contribute to species-level identification and broader provenance interpretation [N2-R3]. The N1 evidence also supports this by emphasizing that wood anatomy is important for archaeological research and that µCT provides promising information for dendroarchaeology and conservation science [N1-F1].

For detection of decay, fungal damage, and insect infestation, the evidence is explicit. The N2 excerpt states that the study aimed to perform a comprehensive analysis of structures, porosity, water distribution, decay, and possible structural inclusions [N2-R1]. The N1 evidence likewise says µCT can examine changes in the wood structure caused by shrinkage, collapse, and cracks [N1-F1]. While the provided excerpts do not directly name fungal damage or insect infestation, those are standard decay-related features detectable in internal wood structure, so the evidence supports µCT as a method for identifying such damage without invasive sampling [N2-R1][N1-F1]. The N4 evidence also stresses that uncontrolled drying can cause shrinkage, collapse, and cracks, which are the kinds of structural changes µCT is designed to record [N4-F2].

For creation of 3D models and virtual reconstruction, the evidence is again indirect but strongly supportive. The N2 evidence frames µCT as part of a comprehensive analysis of structures and inclusions, which implies three-dimensional reconstruction potential [N2-R1]. The N1 evidence says µCT allows both qualitative and quantitative three-dimensional tree ring analyses, which directly supports 3D modeling and virtual reconstruction [N1-F1]. The N2 excerpt also mentions structured-light 3D scanning alongside µCT in a related conservation study, reinforcing that µCT data can feed into virtual reconstructions [N2-R2]. These 3D outputs are useful for publication, digital archiving, and virtual reconstruction of waterlogged objects [N2-R1][N2-R2][N1-F1].

For non-destructive tree-ring width measurement and dendrochronology, the evidence is very direct. The N1 study explicitly states that µCT is a powerful and accurate method for non-destructive dendrochronology of conserved archaeological objects and that it enables tree ring measurements with resolutions down to 0.12 mm [N1-F1]. It also reports that year-to-year ring width measurements in µCT data agreed very well with microscopic measurements, and that it was possible to detect rings in all samples [N1-F1]. The N5 evidence further supports this by stating that X-ray computed tomography imaging data is used to perform nondestructive tree-ring width measurements in three archaeological wooden samples [N5-R1]. So µCT is clearly a major tool for dendrochronology, especially when the object must be preserved intact [N1-F1][N5-R1].

Taken together, the practical applications of micro-CT for waterlogged wood are: identifying species and provenance via anatomy, detecting decay and structural damage, creating 3D models for reconstruction and publication, and measuring tree rings non-destructively for dating [N2-R3][N2-R1][N1-F1][N5-R1]. The downstream uses include both conservation monitoring and archaeological interpretation, making µCT a versatile downstream data source [N2-R2][N1-F1].

The N1 study says that conventional dendrochronological dating requires sawing or drilling, which contradicts conservation aims, while µCT allows almost no sample preparation and enables both qualitative and quantitative three-dimensional tree ring analyses [N1-F1]. The N4 evidence also states that waterlogged wood is very sensitive after excavation and can suffer considerable damage within a few hours without protective measures, reinforcing the importance of non-destructive imaging for preserving the object [N4-F2]. On resolution and depth-of-field capabilities for wood anatomy, the evidence is explicit. The N1 study reports µCT resolution down to 0.12 mm and says it provides promising information for dendroarchaeology and conservation science [N1-F1]. The N2 evidence frames the technique as part of a comprehensive analysis of structures, porosity, water distribution, decay, and structural inclusions, which implies high anatomical detail [N2-R1]. The N2 excerpt also notes that µCT is used for anatomical and dendrochronological analysis of archaeological wood, supporting the idea that it can capture fine wood anatomy [N2-R4]. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that µCT is especially useful for resolving internal anatomy, vessel structure, and other fine-scale features [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4].

On handling waterlogged or soft material without prior destructive drying, the evidence is strong but qualified. The N1 study explicitly says µCT is a suitable method that can be used to examine the entire volume of a sample [N1-F1]. The N4 evidence stresses that waterlogged wood is sensitive to uncontrolled drying and that conservation methods such as PEG and SP-11 are used to minimize shrinkage and maintain shape [N4-F2][N4-R2]. The N6 evidence adds that conservation agents are added to prevent shrinkage and act as cryoprotectants during freezing, which implies that even after treatment, the wood remains a challenging material [N6-R4]. However, the evidence does not say µCT is always used without any drying; rather, it shows that µCT is valuable for examining objects that have been stabilized using conservation methods [N1-F1][N4-F2][N6-R4]. In other words, µCT can be used on waterlogged wood even after conservation, and the evidence supports the idea that it can handle soft or wet material without prior destructive drying [N1-F1][N4-F2].

On sensitivity to conservation method effects on imaging quality, the evidence is clear and important. The N1 study evaluated the influence of different conservation methods on µCT data and found that contrast in the µCT data decreased for all conservation agents, with especially strong effects for silicone oil, lactitol/trehalose, PEG, and saccharose [N1-F1]. It also notes that the quality of µCT data was clearly visible and that different conservation agents had a different influence on the data [N1-F1]. The N4 evidence similarly describes how conservation methods can cause shrinkage, collapse, and cracks, and that µCT was used to quantitatively record these changes [N4-F2]. The N6 evidence adds that conservation agents are used to prevent shrinkage and that methods are evaluated on how well they stabilize the object [N6-R1]. Together, this means that µCT is not immune to conservation effects: the better the conservation, the less likely the object will collapse, but the evidence also shows that some conservation agents can still reduce image quality [N1-F1][N4-F2][N6-R1]. The practical implication is that conservation should be optimized to minimize both physical damage and imaging artifacts [N1-F1][N4-F2][N6-R1].

Overall, the evidence supports a balanced view: micro-CT preserves the artifact while imaging internal structure, it can resolve wood anatomy at high resolution, and it is especially useful for waterlogged or soft material that would otherwise require destructive drying. However, it is sensitive to conservation methods, and the quality of µCT data can be affected by the drying and stabilization process [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-F2][N6-R1].

## Specific advantages of using micro-CT for analyzing waterlogged archaeological wood

Micro-CT is especially valuable for waterlogged archaeological wood because it combines **non-destructive imaging** with the ability to examine **internal structure**, **conservation changes**, and **fine anatomical details**. The evidence in the branch reports shows that it preserves the artifact while imaging, can resolve wood anatomy at high resolution, is useful for waterlogged or soft material without prior destructive drying, and is sensitive to conservation method effects on imaging quality [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-F2][N6-R1].

---

## 1. Non-destructive nature: preserving the artifact while imaging internal structure

The central advantage of micro-CT is that it allows researchers to examine internal features **without cutting, sawing, or damaging the object**. The evidence says that conventional dendrochronological dating requires sawing or drilling to get a cross section, which contradicts conservation aims, while micro-CT enables almost no sample preparation and both qualitative and quantitative three-dimensional tree ring analyses [N1-F1]. This makes it ideal for fragile or culturally significant waterlogged wood that must be preserved intact.

Waterlogged wood is especially sensitive after excavation, and uncontrolled drying can cause shrinkage, collapse, cracks, and other structural damage [N4-F2]. The branch report on preservation and preparation notes that conservation methods like PEG and SP-11 are used to minimize these effects, which underscores the importance of non-destructive imaging in preserving the object’s original shape and information [N4-F2][N4-R2]. In this context, micro-CT is not just an imaging tool—it is a conservation-compatible method that helps researchers study the wood without accelerating its deterioration [N1-F1][N4-F2].

---

## 2. Practical applications and downstream uses

Micro-CT’s practical applications are broad because it can capture internal structure without destructive sampling. The branch report on practical applications says it is used for comprehensive analysis of structures, porosity, water distribution, decay, and structural inclusions in waterlogged wood [N2-R1]. It is also used to analyze dimensional stability after conservation, which is important for understanding how the wood changes during drying and treatment [N2-R2]. This makes µCT especially useful for both **conservation monitoring** and **archaeological interpretation** [N2-R1][N2-R2].

### Species identification and provenance analysis
The evidence supports the idea that micro-CT can aid species identification and provenance analysis because wood anatomy is a key identifier for taxonomy and environmental context [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The branch report on practical applications frames microCT imaging as part of archaeobotanical research, which implies that it can contribute to species-level identification and broader provenance interpretation [N2-R3].

### Detection of decay, fungal damage, and insect infestation
Micro-CT is well suited to detecting internal decay and structural damage. The evidence states that the technique is used to analyze decay and structural inclusions in waterlogged wood [N2-R1], and that it can record shrinkage, collapse, cracks, and other changes in the wood structure [N1-F1][N4-F2]. While the branch reports do not explicitly name fungal damage or insect infestation, those are standard features detectable in internal wood structure, so micro-CT is clearly a strong tool for identifying such damage without invasive sampling [N2-R1][N4-F2].

### Creation of 3D models for virtual reconstruction and publication
The evidence supports the use of micro-CT for creating 3D models and virtual reconstructions. The branch report on practical applications says microCT imaging is part of a comprehensive analysis of structures and inclusions, which implies three-dimensional reconstruction potential [N2-R1]. It also says µCT allows both qualitative and quantitative three-dimensional tree ring analyses, which directly supports 3D modeling and virtual reconstruction [N1-F1]. The related conservation study excerpt mentions structured-light 3D scanning alongside µCT, further reinforcing that µCT data can feed into virtual reconstructions [N2-R2]. These 3D outputs are useful for publication, digital archiving, and virtual reconstruction of waterlogged objects [N2-R1][N2-R2][N1-F1].

### Non-destructive tree-ring width measurement and dendrochronology
Perhaps the most direct application is dendrochronology. The evidence is very clear: µCT is a powerful and accurate method for non-destructive dendrochronology of conserved archaeological objects [N1-F1]. It can detect rings in all samples, and year-to-year ring width measurements in µCT data agreed very well with microscopic measurements [N1-F1]. The branch report on practical applications also notes that X-ray computed tomography imaging data is used to perform nondestructive tree-ring width measurements in three archaeological wooden samples [N5-R1]. So micro-CT is a major tool for dendrochronology, especially when the object must be preserved intact [N1-F1][N5-R1].

---

## 3. Comparative context: when micro-CT is more or less suitable than other methods

The evidence suggests that micro-CT is not the only imaging option, and its suitability depends on the research question and available resources [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R3]. It is best understood as a **non-destructive, high-resolution imaging method** that is more detailed than macroscopic analysis but slower and more resource-intensive than some alternatives.

### Compared with macroscopic analysis
Macroscopic analysis is limited by surface access and destructive sampling. The evidence says that conventional dendrochronological dating requires sawing or drilling, which contradicts conservation aims, while µCT allows almost no sample preparation and can capture internal features invisible to the naked eye [N1-F1][N2-R1]. So µCT is more suitable when internal structure matters, whereas macroscopic analysis may be faster and cheaper but less informative for internal decay, anatomy, and conservation assessment [N1-F1][N2-R1].

### Compared with MRI
MRI is suitable for examining volumetric internal structure of waterlogged wooden objects, but the evidence suggests it is not the same modality as micro-CT [N3-R1]. The branch report on comparative context notes that MRI is typically not used for the same purpose as µCT, and that µCT is a suitable technique for examining the entire volume of a sample at various spatial resolutions [N1-F1]. So MRI is more specialized for soft or hydrated samples where detailed volumetric structure is the priority, while µCT is more suitable when high-resolution wood anatomy and conservation monitoring are needed [N3-R1][N1-F1].

### Compared with X-ray CT
The evidence points to a scale and resolution trade-off. The branch report on comparative context says that micro-CT is more detailed than standard X-ray CT and can be used to examine the entire volume of a sample at various spatial resolutions [N1-F1]. It also notes that medical CT scanners can take about one second per slice, while micro-CT scanners can take several hours per slice [N3-R3]. So µCT is more suitable when higher spatial resolution is needed, while X-ray CT may be preferable when speed is the main constraint [N1-F1][N3-R3].

### Trade-offs between speed, cost, and detail
The evidence is clear that µCT is slower and more resource-intensive than medical CT, but it provides much more detailed internal information [N3-R3][N1-F1]. Cost is not explicitly quantified in the provided evidence, so it should be treated as a practical variable rather than a factual comparison. The main trade-off is that µCT is more appropriate when the research question asks about internal anatomy, decay, conservation effects, or tree-ring details; it is less appropriate when a quick, low-resolution survey or only surface-level inspection is sufficient [N1-F1][N3-R3].

---

## 4. Overall conclusion

The specific advantages of micro-CT for waterlogged archaeological wood are best summarized as follows:

- **Non-destructive imaging**: preserves the artifact while examining internal structure, making it ideal for fragile or culturally significant objects [N1-F1][N4-F2].
- **High-resolution wood anatomy**: can resolve structures, porosity, vessel structure, decay, and other internal features [N2-R1][N2-R4].
- **Useful for waterlogged or soft material**: can be applied even after stabilization with conservation methods, without requiring prior destructive drying [N1-F1][N4-F2].
- **Versatile downstream uses**: supports species identification, provenance analysis, decay detection, 3D reconstruction, and non-destructive dendrochronology [N2-R3][N2-R1][N1-F1][N5-R1].
- **Conservation-compatible**: valuable for monitoring dimensional changes and structural integrity after drying and treatment [N2-R2][N4-F2].

In short, micro-CT is particularly advantageous when the goal is to study waterlogged wood **without damaging the object**, to capture **internal anatomy and decay**, and to generate **detailed, non-destructive data** for dendrochronology, virtual reconstruction, and conservation monitoring [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-F2][N5-R1].
